text.en: Two clues: a concept from ancient Indian mathematicians that adds value to numbers and makes modern calculation possible, and an ancient Indian practice, now popular worldwide, for physical and mental well-being. The answers are zero and yoga. In this story by Anita Rau Badami, a fourteen-year-old tells how her younger brother Anand tries to invent things, with funny and surprising results.

You guess inventions from clues, discuss what the world would be like without inventions and discoveries, and fill a grid with missing letters to form words that show qualities of an inventor, such as creativity, curiosity, imagination and determination.
The story is told by Anita, who is fourteen. Her brother Anand, a year younger, thinks he is a scientist. He loves tinkering with electrical gadgets, tools, dynamos and planks of wood, and his inventions never work as planned. One day their father roars from the front door because a bag of water has fallen on him. Anita hisses that it is Anand's burglar alarm, and he is getting ready to disappear. Their mother finds Papa sopping wet and scowling. Anand's blueprint shows doors, wires and bells. When the door opens, the alarm clangs and a water bag falls on the thief's head, and then they can call the police. He says the alarm works only when the door is opened gently, as a thief would do. Anita is sceptical but keeps quiet and warns him not to involve her. Papa, who always opens the door softly, gets drenched. For a week, Anand does not try anything new.
Then the family watches the film Back to the Future, about a time machine, and the peace of the house ends. Anand's room turns into a network of wires, springs, levers and bulbs, with a huge control switchboard, and he does not even comb his hair. After a fortnight, he announces at lunch that the time machine is ready. Papa says firmly no, and Anand protests that it is an invention. Ma sees his crestfallen look and persuades Papa to at least look at it. The next day Papa and Ma go to Kharagpur for a wedding, for one night. Anita says they can look after themselves and go next door to Sharma Aunty if needed. Ma makes Anand promise not to touch the time machine, which he does half-heartedly, feeling his creation is not respected.
That night Anand falls asleep and Anita stays up reading a murder story. She hears scratching at the front door and then a rattle and a click. Frightened, she wakes Anand, who mutters groggily at first. The door swings open, and they see Boppa, a rough-looking man with a green scarf who had recently begun sweeping the compounds in their row of houses. He had picked a time when the family was out. He threatens them with his cudgel and bolts the door from outside. He comes back and asks which is their father's room. Anita is about to point upstairs, but Anand quickly says it is the one next to theirs, which is his time-machine room. Anita is angry, but Anand says it will give them time. Soon there is a crash and a scream, then muffled thumps, an eerie whine and a low humming. Anand gasps that Boppa has started his time machine. They shout for help. The neighbours, Mr. and Mrs. Sharma and Dr. Mohan, come running and unlock the door. The children explain hurriedly, and the time machine is still humming softly, but Boppa is gone. They search the house and find nothing.
Mrs. Sharma thinks he must have run out and been missed, but Anand insists he disappeared into the past through the time machine. Mr. Sharma smiles indulgently at his imagination and stays the night to guard them. Boppa is never seen again. Papa has the time machine dismantled because he thinks it unsafe, and maybe because he has a niggling suspicion that it worked. Anand is convinced he is a genius and starts a new project, a telephone to contact creatures in outer space.
The cause-and-effect pairs are: Anand rigged the alarm to work on a soft opening, so Papa got soaked; Anita avoided blame because Anand faced the consequences; they saw Back to the Future, so Anand built a time machine; Papa said no because he feared it was unsafe. Anand did not keep his promise completely. He did not use the machine, but it was used by Boppa, though not through his own action. He gave a half-hearted promise and then led Boppa into the time-machine room. The correct order is: Anita wakes Anand; the door swings open and Boppa stands there; Anand misleads Boppa into the time-machine room; the neighbours unlock the door. The narrator introduces herself and her brother to put the reader in the picture. The tone is humorous. Anand is imaginative, inventive and stubborn, and Anita is practical and sceptical.
Words in the text include racket, a loud disturbing noise; sopping, soaking; scowling, having an angry look; tinkering, experimenting; rigged up, assembled temporarily; sceptical, doubtful; stealthily, quietly so as not to be seen; crestfallen, sad and disappointed; brandishing, waving; cudgel, a short thick stick; groggily, sleepily; and indulgently, fondly. Repeated structures such as as angry as angry could be and as mad as mad can be show strong feeling, and words like clanging, humming and clattering are sound words that make the story vivid.
